title: The Wire That Snapped

patient.name: Mr Muhammad Hafiz bin Yusof
patient.presenting_complaint: A metal wire snapped and flew into his right eye while cutting cable ties on site about 30 minutes ago
patient.address: Blk 128 Ang Mo Kio Ave 3, #11-547, Singapore 554133

history.hpc: Mr Hafiz was using wire cutters when a piece of taut metal wire snapped back and struck his right eye. He felt immediate sharp pain and noticed his vision in that eye became blurry straight away. His supervisor brought him to SNEC directly. He has not touched or rubbed the eye. He reports the eye is watering and feels like 'something is stuck inside'. He did not vomit and has no headache.
history.pmhx: Nil significant. No previous eye conditions. Last tetanus vaccination unknown — needs to be checked.
history.social_hx: Construction worker. Was not wearing protective eyewear. Came in with supervisor.

iop.right: Not measured — IOP and any contact procedures are CONTRAINDICATED if penetrating injury suspected

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Right eye: irregular, peaked pupil, visible small dark area at the limbus suggestive of a full-thickness wound with possible uveal prolapse, mild hyphaema. A small metallic fragment appears to be protruding from the globe. Left eye: normal.
examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed — any pressure on the globe is contraindicated

investigations.va_distance: RE: CF at 1m. LE: 6/6. Performed gently without applying any pressure to the right eye or lids.
investigations.external_inspection: Irregular peaked pupil, possible globe perforation with foreign body in situ — visual inspection only, no instruments or drops applied to right eye

diagnosis: Suspected penetrating eye injury (PEI) with intraocular foreign body, right eye. Triage Category 1 — do NOT touch the eye, apply protective shield, and get the patient to the doctor within 10 minutes.

immediate: Recognise this as a Category 1 emergency — penetrating eye injury with possible retained foreign body
DO NOT touch, press on, or attempt to remove the foreign body or examine closely with instruments
DO NOT instil any eye drops, perform NCT, or apply any pressure to the right eye
Apply a rigid protective shield (e.g. an eye shield or a cut-out cup) over the right eye without touching the globe — secure it so it rests on the bony orbital rim, not the eye itself
Alert the doctor and nurse-in-charge immediately — this patient must be seen within 10 minutes
Keep the patient calm, seated or lying still, and instruct him not to cough, strain, squeeze his eyes shut, or rub the eye
Ask about tetanus immunisation status and last meal/drink (in case surgery under GA is needed) and inform the doctor
Document mechanism of injury, time of injury, visual acuity, and time the patient was seen
follow_up: Doctor will arrange urgent imaging (CT orbit) to localise the foreign body
Likely referral for emergency surgical exploration and foreign body removal under GA
Keep patient fasted (NBM) once injury is confirmed, in case surgery is required
IV antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis as ordered by doctor
patient_education: Reassure the patient that the team is acting quickly to protect his eye
Explain why he must not rub, squeeze, or press on the eye — this could worsen the injury and push contents out of the eye
Advise him to remain calm and avoid straining or coughing forcefully
Explain that he will likely need to remain fasted in case surgery is needed

key_points: Asks about mechanism and time of injury (high-velocity metal fragment)
Asks whether the patient has touched, rubbed, or attempted to remove anything from the eye
Asks about last oral intake (relevant for possible GA/surgery)
Recognises history alone (mechanism + sudden visual drop) is enough to suspect PEI without further provocation
Tests VA gently in both eyes without applying pressure to the injured eye
Recognises NCT/IOP measurement is contraindicated when PEI is suspected
Avoids instilling any drops or touching the globe with instruments
Documents the irregular pupil and visible foreign body by observation only
Identifies this as a suspected penetrating eye injury with intraocular foreign body
Recognises irregular/peaked pupil and visible fragment as classic PEI signs
Understands the 'do not touch' principle for self-evident penetrating injuries
Applies a protective shield without pressing on the globe
Does not instil drops, perform NCT, or otherwise manipulate the eye
Alerts doctor/nurse-in-charge immediately and escalates as Category 1
Checks tetanus status and fasting status and communicates these to the team
Keeps the patient calm and still to avoid increasing intraocular pressure or extruding contents
